title: What you practice
hookLine: list the practices that became yours
tomorrow: a practice wants people. so where do you belong?

cards: Noa's packing list for college has a section her mom didn't expect: two candlesticks, a small mezuzah, the kiddush cup Saba gave her. Nobody told her to pack them. They're just what she does now.
A habit app would call them streaks. The Torah has an older way to say it, from the day at Sinai, and the order of the words is the surprise.

teach.h: WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.
teach.b: Moses reads the covenant to the people, and they answer: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew, na'aseh v'nishma: we will do, and we will hear. Doing comes first.
The Talmud tells that when Israel put we will do before we will hear, angels came down and gave each person two crowns, one for each word.
Pirkei Avot says it in plain prose: Shimon, son of Rabban Gamliel, taught that study isn't the main thing; the doing is.
The tradition prizes study too, but it trusts that understanding often grows out of practice, not only the other way around. So what are your practices, honestly? Maybe a blessing before food.
Words of thanks before getting out of bed. A coin in a box before Shabbat. Candles on Friday.
Ten minutes with a text. The list may be short. That's fine.
A short, true list is a portrait of a life.
Something to tell a friend tonight: at Sinai, the people promised to do before they promised to understand.

how: Jews keep practices at many different levels: lighting Shabbat candles, saying blessings over food, putting up a mezuzah, giving tzedakah, studying; the phrase na'aseh v'nishma is often quoted for the idea that doing leads to understanding.

practice: On paper, list the practices that are actually yours now, small ones included: a blessing, a candle, a coin, a text you open. Then put a star next to the one you'd keep if you could keep only one.
